deck.title: EBS, EFS & Instance Store
deck.analogy: Your instance is a desk in an office: EBS is your personal external hard drive, EFS is the shared network folder the whole office mounts, and Instance Store is the notepad glued to the desk.

subtopics.title: Instance Store: the notepad glued to the desk

cards.front: What are the three EC2 storage personalities?

back.answer: EBS = private and persistent, EFS = shared, Instance Store = fast but disposable.
back.mnemonic: Desk in an office: EBS = personal external hard drive, EFS = the office's shared network folder, Instance Store = notepad glued to the desk.

cards.front: Where does an EBS volume live, and how do you move it to another AZ?

back.answer: It lives in exactly one AZ; snapshot it and restore the snapshot in the target AZ.

cards.examTip: move volume across AZ → snapshot → restore

cards.front: How many EC2 instances can attach the same EBS volume at once, and what is the exception?

back.answer: One at a time — except io1/io2 Multi-Attach: up to 16 instances in the same AZ.
back.explanation: Multi-Attach is for cluster-aware software only, not ordinary filesystems.

cards.examTip: multiple instances, one block volume, same AZ → io1/io2 Multi-Attach (max 16)

cards.front: Does an EBS volume keep its data if the EC2 instance it is attached to is terminated?

back.answer: Yes — EBS persists independently of the instance; only the DeleteOnTermination flag can delete it.

cards.front: What are the DeleteOnTermination defaults for EBS root volumes vs extra attached volumes?

back.answer: Root volume: true by default (lost on termination); extra volumes: false (they survive).
back.explanation: To make the root volume survive termination, turn DeleteOnTermination off.

cards.examTip: "root volume must survive termination" → DeleteOnTermination = false

cards.front: Why is a freshly attached extra EBS volume unusable until you act?

back.answer: It is a raw disk: you must format it, mount it, and add it to /etc/fstab yourself.
back.explanation: Without the fstab entry it vanishes from the mount table on reboot.

cards.examTip: new extra volume unusable → format + mount + fstab

cards.front: EBS performance: IOPS vs throughput — which workloads want which?

back.answer: IOPS = many small random reads/writes (databases); throughput = large sequential MB/s (big data, log processing, ETL, streaming).

cards.examTip: random I/O → SSD; large sequential → HDD

cards.front: To save money, can an EC2 instance boot from a cheap st1 or sc1 HDD volume?

back.answer: No — HDD volumes (st1/sc1) can never be boot volumes; boot requires SSD (gp3 or io1/io2).

cards.examTip: st1/sc1 → never bootable

cards.front: Which EBS volume types cover ≤16,000 IOPS vs above?

back.answer: gp3 handles up to 16,000 IOPS cheaply; above 16,000 only io1/io2 (provisioned IOPS) works.
back.explanation: io2 Block Express reaches 256,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency.

cards.examTip: the 16,000 IOPS threshold decides most questions

cards.front: gp2 vs gp3: how do IOPS work on each?

back.answer: gp2 chains IOPS to size (3 IOPS per GB, bursts to 3,000); gp3 gives a 3,000 IOPS + 125 MB/s baseline at any size.

cards.front: gp2 vs gp3: how do you scale performance on each?

back.answer: gp2 forces buying more storage to get more IOPS; gp3 provisions IOPS and throughput independently of size.

cards.examTip: more IOPS without more storage → gp3

cards.front: gp2 vs gp3: which is cheaper?

back.answer: gp3 — about 20% cheaper than gp2.
back.explanation: The moment a question mentions gp2, the answer is almost always migrate to gp3.

cards.examTip: gp2 mentioned → migrate to gp3

cards.front: How do EBS snapshots work and where are they stored?

back.answer: Incremental backups stored in S3 — after the first snapshot, only changed blocks are saved, so they are cheap.

cards.front: How do you back up EBS data to another region for disaster recovery?

back.answer: Take a snapshot and copy it to the other region.

cards.examTip: back up EBS to another region → snapshot copy

cards.front: What is the EBS Snapshot Archive tier?

back.answer: ~75% cheaper snapshot storage, but restores take 24–72 hours.

cards.examTip: rarely restored, minimize snapshot cost

cards.front: What protects against accidentally deleted EBS snapshots?

back.answer: Recycle Bin — retention rules that keep deleted snapshots recoverable.

cards.examTip: recover deleted snapshot → Recycle Bin

cards.front: What does Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) do?

back.answer: Pre-warms a volume restored from a snapshot for full performance instantly — but it is expensive.
back.explanation: Normal restores load blocks lazily, so the first read of each block is slow.

cards.examTip: no latency on first access after restore → FSR

cards.front: Which service automates EBS snapshot creation, retention, and deletion on a schedule?

back.answer: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM).

cards.examTip: "automate EBS backups" → DLM

cards.front: An EBS volume is encrypted — what about its snapshots and volumes restored from them?

back.answer: All encrypted: encryption is inherited downstream (encrypted volume → encrypted snapshots → encrypted volumes).

cards.front: How do you encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume?

back.answer: Snapshot it → copy the snapshot with encryption enabled → create a new volume from the encrypted copy → swap it in.
back.explanation: You cannot flip encryption on in place — the snapshot-copy dance is the only way.
back.code: unencrypted volume → snapshot → copy (enable encryption) → create volume from encrypted copy → swap in

cards.examTip: "encrypt existing volume" → snapshot → copy-encrypted → restore

cards.front: What is Amazon EFS, protocol-wise?

back.answer: A managed NFS (Network File System) — the classic Linux shared-folder protocol.
back.mnemonic: EFS = the shared network folder the whole office mounts.

cards.front: How does EFS mounting differ from EBS attachment?

back.answer: EFS is mounted by many instances at once across multiple AZs; EBS is one instance (mostly) in one AZ.

cards.examTip: many Linux instances, multi-AZ, shared files → EFS

cards.front: Windows EC2 instances need shared file storage with Active Directory — should they mount EFS?

back.answer: No — EFS is Linux-only. Use FSx for Windows File Server (SMB protocol, Active Directory integration).

cards.examTip: read the OS in the question before answering EFS

cards.front: How does EFS capacity and pricing work?

back.answer: Elastic — it auto-grows and shrinks; you pay per GB actually used, no capacity planning.
back.explanation: Pricier per GB than EBS, but you buy zero unused space, and lifecycle tiers claw back cost.

cards.front: EFS performance modes: when do you pick Max I/O over General Purpose?

back.answer: Max I/O for thousands of concurrent clients that tolerate higher latency (big data); General Purpose is the default.

cards.examTip: thousands of concurrent clients → Max I/O

cards.front: Which EFS throughput mode is the recommended default?

back.answer: Elastic — it auto-scales throughput with demand (alternatives: Provisioned and Bursting).

cards.examTip: EFS throughput default → Elastic

cards.front: How do you cut EFS cost for files that go cold?

back.answer: Lifecycle policies auto-move files Standard → Infrequent Access → Archive, saving ~90%+ on IA.

cards.examTip: files untouched for months → lifecycle to IA/Archive

cards.front: What is Instance Store and how fast is it?

back.answer: Physical disk inside the host machine — the fastest storage EC2 offers; NVMe instance store reaches millions of IOPS.
back.explanation: No network hop at all, far beyond anything EBS can do.
back.mnemonic: The notepad glued to the desk itself.

cards.sourceHeading: Instance Store: the notepad glued to the desk
cards.examTip: fastest storage → Instance Store

cards.front: When is Instance Store data lost, and when does it survive?

back.answer: Lost when the instance stops, hibernates, or terminates; it survives a reboot.
back.explanation: A reboot stays on the same host; a stop can move you to a different one — and someone else's desk has a different notepad.

cards.sourceHeading: Instance Store: the notepad glued to the desk
cards.examTip: stop/terminate = data gone; reboot survives

cards.front: Can an Instance Store volume be detached, snapshotted, or resized?

back.answer: No — it cannot be detached or snapshotted via EBS mechanisms, and its size is fixed by the instance type.

cards.sourceHeading: Instance Store: the notepad glued to the desk

cards.front: What are legitimate uses for Instance Store?

back.answer: Cache, buffer, scratch space, temp processing files, or data replicated at the application layer anyway (e.g. Cassandra nodes).

cards.sourceHeading: Instance Store: the notepad glued to the desk
cards.examTip: cache / scratch / replicated data → Instance Store is OK

cards.front: A workload needs the highest possible IOPS and the data must persist — is Instance Store the answer?

back.answer: No — instance store wins the IOPS contest but flunks persistence; choose io2 Block Express EBS.

cards.sourceHeading: Instance Store: the notepad glued to the desk
cards.examTip: the word "persist" disqualifies instance store instantly

cards.front: Five-storage lineup: which storage is fastest, physical, ephemeral — cache/scratch/replicated data only?

back.answer: Instance Store.

cards.front: Five-storage lineup: which storage is a network block device, one instance (mostly), one AZ, persistent — boot volumes and databases?

back.answer: EBS.

cards.front: Five-storage lineup: which storage is a shared NFS folder, multi-AZ, many Linux instances, pay-per-use — shared content?

back.answer: EFS.

cards.front: Five-storage lineup: which storage provides managed third-party file systems — Windows (SMB/AD) or Lustre for HPC?

back.answer: FSx (FSx for Windows File Server, FSx for Lustre).

cards.front: Five-storage lineup: which storage is object storage over HTTP — not a disk at all, effectively unlimited?

back.answer: S3 — apps talk to it via API.

cards.front: A database needs 12,000 IOPS and the solution must be cost-effective. Which EBS volume type?

back.answer: gp3 — 12,000 is under the 16,000 line, and gp3 provisions IOPS cheaply.

choices.why: Overkill and expensive — gp3 covers up to 16,000 IOPS.
12,000 is under the 16,000 IOPS line; gp3 provisions IOPS cheaply.
HDD is for sequential throughput, not database random I/O.
Cold HDD — lowest performance, not for databases.

cards.examTip: "12,000 IOPS, cost-effective" → gp3

cards.front: A critical database needs 50,000 IOPS. Which EBS volume type?

back.answer: io1/io2 — past 16,000, only provisioned-IOPS SSD plays.
back.explanation: Sub-millisecond latency or 256k IOPS → io2 Block Express.

choices.why: Caps at 16,000 IOPS.
HDD throughput, not high random IOPS.
Past 16,000 IOPS only provisioned-IOPS SSD plays.
Ephemeral — data lost on stop; wrong for a critical database.

cards.examTip: "50,000 IOPS" → io1/io2

cards.front: Sequential processing of large log files, throughput-focused, cost-effective — which EBS volume type?

back.answer: st1 — big + sequential = HDD; frequent access = st1.
back.explanation: Cold archive would be sc1 — and neither can boot.

choices.why: SSD random I/O — wastes money on sequential streams.
Big + sequential + frequently accessed = throughput-optimized HDD.
Cold HDD — for infrequently accessed data.
Provisioned-IOPS SSD is the opposite of cost-effective here.

cards.examTip: "sequential, throughput, cost-effective" → st1

cards.front: A gp2 volume needs more IOPS but not more storage. What do you do?

back.answer: Migrate to gp3 — it provisions IOPS independently and is ~20% cheaper.

choices.why: Buys storage you don't need — gp2 chains IOPS to size.
Independent IOPS provisioning and ~20% cheaper.
HDD can't serve random I/O or boot volumes.
Massive overkill for a gp2-scale workload.

cards.examTip: "gp2 needs more IOPS, not storage" → migrate to gp3

cards.front: A fleet of Linux instances in an Auto Scaling Group must all see the same uploaded files. Which storage?

back.answer: EFS — many mounters + multi-AZ + NFS = the shared folder.
back.explanation: Signature use case: user uploads, CMS content, WordPress wp-content.

choices.why: One AZ, max 16, cluster-aware filesystems only.
Many mounters + multi-AZ + NFS = the shared folder.
Ephemeral and per-host — nothing is shared.
Object storage via API, not a mounted shared file system.

cards.examTip: "Linux fleet must share files" → EFS

cards.front: Windows instances need shared storage with Active Directory integration. Which service?

back.answer: FSx for Windows File Server — SMB protocol, AD integration.

choices.why: Linux-only — THE trap.
HPC parallel file system, not SMB/AD.
SMB protocol with Active Directory integration.
Single-instance block storage, not shared.

cards.examTip: "Windows + shared + AD" → FSx for Windows

cards.front: Which storage for the fastest possible temporary scratch/cache data on EC2?

back.answer: Instance Store — "temporary" unlocks it: millions of IOPS, ephemeral is fine here.

choices.why: "Temporary" unlocks it — millions of IOPS, ephemeral is fine.
Fast, but you pay for persistence you don't need.
Network file system — far slower than local NVMe.
HDD — terrible random I/O for scratch work.

cards.examTip: "temporary scratch/cache" → Instance Store

cards.front: A workload needs high-IOPS storage whose data must persist after the instance stops. Which storage?

back.answer: io2 EBS, not instance store — "persist" disqualifies the notepad.

choices.why: Wins IOPS but data dies on stop — "persist" disqualifies it.
Cheapest HDD — low IOPS.
Highest persistent IOPS — Block Express hits 256k IOPS, sub-ms.
Shared file storage, not high-IOPS block storage.

cards.examTip: "high IOPS + must persist" → io2 EBS

cards.front: A data volume must survive instance termination. What do you configure?

back.answer: DeleteOnTermination = false on that volume.
back.explanation: Root defaults true, extra volumes default false — check which one the question means.

choices.why: Root defaults true, extra volumes false — flip the flag.
Sharing a volume says nothing about termination.

choices.text: Move the data to Instance Store
choices.why: Ephemeral — dies with the instance anyway.
Volume type doesn't change the deletion flag.

cards.examTip: "survive termination" → DeleteOnTermination = false

cards.front: You must encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume. How?

back.answer: Snapshot → copy the snapshot with encryption enabled → create a volume from the encrypted copy.

choices.text: Turn on encryption in the volume's settings
choices.why: No in-place flip exists — that's the trap.

choices.text: Snapshot → copy with encryption → create volume from the copy
choices.why: The required snapshot-copy dance.

choices.text: Attach a new encrypted volume and unmount the old one
choices.why: Copies nothing — the data stays unencrypted.

choices.text: Enable account default encryption, then reboot
choices.why: Applies only to newly created volumes.

cards.examTip: "encrypt existing volume" → snapshot-copy dance

cards.front: Back up EBS volumes to another region for DR — automatically. Which approach?

back.answer: DLM-scheduled snapshots + cross-region snapshot copy.
back.explanation: Snapshots live in S3 and copy across regions.

choices.why: Pre-warms restores — performance, not DR automation.

choices.text: Manually copy snapshots on a schedule
choices.why: Works but isn't automatic.
Undelete safety net, not cross-region backup.
Automates snapshots and copies them to the DR region.

cards.examTip: "automated cross-region EBS backup" → DLM + snapshot copy

cards.front: Multiple instances must attach the same block volume in one AZ (cluster software). What do you use?

back.answer: io1/io2 Multi-Attach — up to 16 instances in the same AZ.
back.explanation: It is block storage, not a file system.

choices.why: A file system, not an attached block volume.
Only io1/io2 support Multi-Attach.
Up to 16 instances in the same AZ, cluster-aware software.
Fixed to its host — can't be attached elsewhere.

cards.examTip: "same block volume, one AZ, cluster" → Multi-Attach

cards.front: How do you reduce the cost of EFS for files untouched for months?

back.answer: Lifecycle policy to EFS IA/Archive.
back.explanation: Same trick as S3 tiering, applied to the shared folder.

choices.why: Changes throughput billing, not storage cost.
Auto-moves cold files to cheaper tiers — ~90%+ savings.
Breaks multi-instance shared access.
Performance mode for many clients, not cost tiering.

cards.examTip: "EFS files untouched for months" → IA/Archive lifecycle

back.answer: SSD (gp3 or io1/io2)

back.answer: st1

cards.front: Keyword: **"coldest, cheapest EBS"**

back.answer: sc1

back.answer: migrate to gp3 (~20% cheaper)

back.answer: gp3 (independent provisioning)

cards.front: Keyword: **"multiple instances, one block volume, same AZ"**

back.answer: io1/io2 Multi-Attach (max 16)

cards.front: Keyword: **"root disk survives termination"**

back.answer: DeleteOnTermination = false

cards.front: Keyword: **"new extra volume unusable"**

back.answer: format + mount + fstab

cards.front: Keyword: **"move volume across AZ/region"**

back.answer: snapshot → (copy) → restore

back.answer: Snapshot Archive (75% off, 24–72 hr restore)

cards.front: Keyword: **"recover deleted snapshot"**

cards.front: Keyword: **"instant full performance from snapshot"**

back.answer: Fast Snapshot Restore (expensive)
